tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.

schema.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
schema.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

At most 100 characters.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

=== DECISIONS.md
# Decisions

Numbered, each with its reason. Newest at the bottom.

## Before Step 1 (2026-10-29)

**1. The source is AmericanStories, not the Chronicling America API.**
The old Chronicling America JSON API returns 404. AmericanStories has the same scans as structured article text, under CC-BY-4.0. It also keeps each article's bounding box, which lets the site crop the original clipping from the Library of Congress image service.

**2. Read the whole archive (180 year files), not a sample.**
A full pass is 340 GB. At the measured 66 MB/s that is about 1.5 h of transfer, which is affordable. Full coverage makes the counts honest and lets every US town get its results.

**3. Stream every file and never keep the tarballs.**
The disk has 37 GB free, and the largest year alone is 7.6 GB.

**4. Walks is an optional layer on top of search, and it is built last.**
Halloween and Día de los Muertos are nights when people go out, both to haunted places and to graves. On Oct 29, none of 598 posts offered walks built from original sources. The nearest were GeoLetter (letters left at places) and Trailhead (general outing cards).
Walks also gives two tools a real job:
- SerpApi's Google Maps results answer "is it still standing?"
- Atlas geo queries answer "near me".

Old reports are often vague, and many of the places are gone. So walks use only precisely located public stops, every pin shows how precise it is, and Walks is cut if Steps 1–4 run late.

**5. One main tool (Tinker); the others support it. MongoDB Atlas, not Tiger Data. No .tech domain.**
Week 2's partner winners each made one partner the core of the product and proved it under failure. Our Week 2 entry, Cubby, spread thin uses across seven partners and won nothing. So the depth goes into the Tinker reader, and Atlas, Temporal, Render and Sentry each get one real job.

Why Atlas over Tiger Data:
- Atlas is already set up; Tiger Data would need a new account.
- Articles are JSON documents, and Atlas covers all three searches we need (geo, fuzzy text, vectors) in one place.
- On Oct 29, three entries claimed Tiger Data, including Still Here by the author who won Tiger Data in Week 1.

The owner chose not to use a .tech domain.

=== DECISIONS-append.md

## Planning (2026-10-29)

**6. The build runs in five phases with gates, managed by an EM session.**
`BUILD-PLAN.md` maps the `BRIEF.md` steps onto five phases: scaffolding; database, schemas and data models; backend and APIs; frontend; polish and QA. Each milestone ends at a gate the EM checks before the next one starts. The owner manages the schedule, so whether Walks is built is the owner's call at the Phase 4 gate.

**7. Static-first site: the core path is prebuilt JSON, and the live API handles search, near me and similar.**
Free Render web services sleep after a short idle. A judge's first click has to be instant, and an outage at the API, at Atlas or at LoC shouldn't blank the front page, a town or a case.

**8. Stories and printings are counted separately.**
Syndicated ghost stories were reprinted in many papers. Counting each printing as its own ghost would inflate the numbers and duplicate cases. Reprints of a gold article in the training data would also inflate the reader's scores.

**9. Models are selected on a dev split, and the gold set is used only for final evals.**
That keeps the held-out numbers honest.

**10. The investigator's default model is Gemma 4 26B-A4B (QAT), running locally through Ollama. Ultramarine is the comparison run.**
The model is already on this machine (15 GB), it's open-weight, and it keeps the investigation offline. Both runs work the same cases, so the comparison is fair.

**11. The Halloween look comes from the reading room after dark.**
`UI-IDEAS.md` sets the direction: the lamp, the lights off, and the scans as the only imagery. Costume-shop iconography is out.

**12. Config accepts both names for the Ultramarine key.**
`.env` names it `PAPERINSTRUMENTS_API_KEY`, while `BRIEF.md` says `ULTRAMARINE_API_KEY`. The owner's file stays as it is.

# Resume

Where the build stands, for whoever picks it up next. The spec is `BRIEF.md`, and the reasons behind each choice are in `DECISIONS.md`. Each step ends with a STATUS block below.

## Next step

**Step 1: setup and archive read.**

Hard date: the site must be live on Oct 31, so Steps 1–5 need to fit in about 33 hours.

Already done (Oct 29):
- The private GitHub repo `Hotragn/Paperghosts` is cloned here; its only commit so far is the LICENSE.
- `.gitignore` covers `.env` and keeps `Docs/IDEAS.md` private.
- `.env` holds the keys copied from Week 3 (never displayed).
- Entire session capture is enabled for Claude Code in this repo only. Checkpoints sync to `origin` on push.

Sentry is ready (done Oct 29):
- Projects `paperghosts-api` (Python/FastAPI) and `paperghosts-web` (React) exist in org `hotragn`.
- Their DSNs are in `.env` as `SENTRY_DSN` and `SENTRY_DSN_WEB`. These replaced the old Flare DSN.
- An auth token with read access is in `.env`.
- The GitHub repo is linked in Sentry.
- Wire the SDKs as the code appears.

The build waits on no one. Optional extras that the owner may add later:
- Ultramarine key and SerpApi key (they upgrade Step 4)

Needs the owner's yes when we get there:
- Render deploy
- domain DNS

lines: +# Architecture: Paper Ghosts

+How the system is built and how data moves through it. The spec is `BRIEF.md`, requirements with IDs are in `SRS.md`, and the build order is `BUILD-PLAN.md`. Where this file and `BRIEF.md` disagree, `BRIEF.md` wins and this file gets fixed.
+## 1. Shape of the system
+Two halves that never block each other:

+- **The pipeline (offline, on the owner's Mac, durable on Temporal).** It reads the 340 GB archive, trains and runs the reader, geocodes, loads Atlas, gathers follow-ups and runs the investigator. All AI work happens here. None of it runs when someone visits the site.
+- **The site (online, on Render).** A React static site plus a read-only FastAPI service over MongoDB Atlas.
+  - The core path (front page, town, case) is served from prebuilt static JSON, so a visitor's first click never waits on a sleeping server.
+  - Live features (archive text search, near me, ghosts like this one) call the API.
+Clipping images come straight from the Library of Congress IIIF service. Crops for the front page and the top cases are also cached as static files, so the best material survives an LoC outage.
+```mermaid
+flowchart LR
+  subgraph SRC["Sources"]

+ HF["AmericanStories
180 year files, 340 GB"]
+    GN["GeoNames cities1000"]
+    LOC["LoC IIIF image service"]
+    NOW["SerpApi, Wikipedia"]
+  end
+  subgraph PIPE["Pipeline: owner's Mac, durable on Temporal"]

+ ING["Ingest + prefilter"] --> CAND[("candidates
local .jsonl.zst")]

+ CAND --> TRI["Triage"] --> RDR["Reader
Qwen 4B + LoRA, trained on Tinker"]

+ RDR --> VER["Quote verifier"] --> GEO["Geocoder"] --> CLU["Reprint clustering
+ embeddings"]
+    CLU --> LOAD["Atlas loader"]

+ LOAD --> HARV["Follow-up harvest
second archive pass"] --> INV["Investigator
Gemma 4 local, Ultramarine"]
+    INV --> LOAD
+  end
+  subgraph DB["MongoDB Atlas"]
+    REP[("reports")]
+    CAS[("cases")]
+    PLA[("places")]
+    STA[("stats")]
+  end
+  subgraph SITE["Site: Render"]
+    EXP["Static export, at build time"] --> WEB["React static site"]
+    API["FastAPI, read-only"]
+  end
+  HF --> ING
+  GN --> GEO
+  NOW --> INV
+  LOAD --> DB
+  DB --> EXP
+  DB --> API
+  WEB -- "search, near me, similar" --> API
+  WEB -. "clipping crops" .-> LOC
+  PIPE -. "traces" .-> SEN["Sentry"]
+  SITE -. "errors, traces" .-> SEN
+## 2. Components
+| Component | Job | Built with | Runs |

+| Ingest | Stream each year file, parse pages, prefilter articles, write candidates, counts and recall samples | `httpx` streaming, `tarfile` in `r\|gz` mode, `orjson`, `zstandard` | One Temporal activity per year file |

+| Triage | Drop candidates whose every match is a known idiom ("Holy Ghost", "ghost of a chance", "gave up the ghost"), only if the eval shows it loses no reports | Rules, measured on the gold set | Pipeline |

+| Reader | Classify each candidate and extract fields, each with a verbatim quote | Qwen 4B student with a LoRA trained on Tinker from teacher labels | Full pass on Tinker sampling; also runs locally offline |
+| Quote verifier | Keep a field only if its quote is found in the OCR text, allowing for OCR noise | `rapidfuzz`, threshold calibrated on the gold set | Pipeline and investigator |
+| Geocoder | Publication place from the LCCN title; article places from the reader | GeoNames `cities1000`, offline, with a manifest | Pipeline |
+| Reprint clustering | Group printings of the same story across papers (syndication was common) | Shingles + MinHash, plus a date window | Pipeline |
+| Embedder | Vectors for "ghosts like this one" | An open embedding model through Ollama; dimensions chosen to fit the Atlas budget | Pipeline only; the site reuses stored vectors |
+| Atlas loader | Upsert reports, places, cases and stats; create indexes | PyMongo | Pipeline |
+| Follow-up harvest | Second streaming pass over only the years the top cases need: follow-ups, death notices, inquests, debunkings | The ingest code with per-case patterns | Temporal workflow |

+| Investigator | An agent that writes a case file in which every claim cites a clipping | Gemma 4 26B-A4B through Ollama by default; Ultramarine as the comparison run; tools for archive search, Atlas, SerpApi and Wikipedia | One Temporal workflow per case; every model call and tool call is an activity |
+| Static export | Prebuilt JSON for the front page, the town index, each town, each case and the archive chart | Python script reading Atlas | At deploy time |
+| API | Text search, near me, similar, printed-on-this-night, stats, health | FastAPI, PyMongo async | Render web service |
+| Web | Every page, built on the design system from `UI-IDEAS.md` | React, Vite, TypeScript | Render static site |

+| Observability | Errors and traces, including token counts and cost per model call | Sentry: `paperghosts-api` for the API and the pipeline (tagged by environment), `paperghosts-web` for the site | Everywhere |
+Temporal runs only on the owner's machine, through the CLI dev server. The live site never needs it.
+## 3. Data flow, step by step
+### 3.1 Ingest (`IngestArchiveWorkflow`)
+- **Input:** a list of years, all 180 by default.
+- **Output per year, under `data/`:**
+  - `candidates/{year}.jsonl.zst`: articles that hit the lexicon, with the matched terms, page metadata and scan location
+  - `counts/{year}.json`: pages, articles and candidates, broken down by state and by term

+  - `samples/{year}.jsonl.zst`: a reservoir sample of non-candidates, plus a near-miss pool (articles with words like "knocking", "strange noises" or "spirits" but no ghost term). Both feed the recall measurement.
+  - `manifests/{year}.json`: source URL, bytes read, lexicon version, code version, start and finish times
+- **One activity per year file:** stream, gunzip, and read tar members one at a time. The tarball never touches the disk.
+  - Heartbeats carry progress (members done, bytes read).
+  - Retry policy: exponential backoff with a bounded number of attempts.
+- **Idempotent:**
+  - Outputs are written to a temporary file and renamed when complete.
+  - A year whose manifest matches the current lexicon and code versions is skipped.
+  - A killed worker re-runs only unfinished years. The year in flight restarts from its beginning, because a gzip stream can't seek. The kill-test write-up says so.
+- **Concurrency:** bounded, starting from what Phase 1 measures for download speed and parse speed on this machine (10 cores).
+- **Disk:** about 35 GB is free, so all ingest outputs together must stay under 10 GB, measured and reported.
+### 3.2 Gold set and reader
+- **Gold set:**
+  - 150–300 candidates, stratified by decade and lexicon term and including near-miss items.
+  - Frozen before any training: the split and its hash are committed under `eval/gold/`.
+  - The build agent labels it before seeing any model output, from the OCR text and the scan crop where the OCR is unclear.
+  - The labelling rules for hard cases (séance reports, reprinted fiction, hoax exposures, humour columns) are written in `eval/gold/POLICY.md` before labelling starts.
+- **Training data:** the teacher labels a separate pool. No gold article, and no reprint of a gold article, may appear in it.
+- **Model selection** happens on a dev split. The gold set is touched only for final evaluations.
+- **Full pass:** the tuned student reads every triaged candidate and writes `data/reader/{year}.jsonl.zst`. Every field either passes the quote verifier or becomes "not stated".
+### 3.3 Geocode, cluster, embed, load
+- Places are resolved against GeoNames. Every location records its precision (town, street or building) and its source. Street or building coordinates exist only when a source supplies them.
+- Printings of the same story are grouped. Counts on the site say which they count: stories or printings.
+- Stories get one embedding each, from the earliest legible printing.
+- The loader upserts by stable IDs, so re-running it is safe.
+### 3.4 Follow-up harvest
+- The top 30–60 cases are picked by a written, versioned rule: a verified place, named people or a specific place, and a legible clipping.
+- The years those cases need are grouped, and each year file is streamed once.
+- From each stream, the harvest pulls articles that match a case's named people, its specific place, or its town within a date window.
+- Output goes to `data/harvest/{case_id}.jsonl`.
+### 3.5 Investigator (the main Temporal story)
+- `InvestigateCaseWorkflow(case_id, model)` runs a loop: plan, call tools, read, write claims, verify.
+  - Every model call and every tool call is an activity, with an idempotency key made from the workflow ID and the step number.
+  - Temporal records each result in the workflow history. After a crash the workflow replays and reuses those results, so no completed model call or web search is repeated.

+  - A call that is in flight when the worker dies has no recorded result, so Temporal retries it. The idempotency key lets a provider that supports one drop the duplicate, and the kill test counts these retries rather than claiming there are none.
+- **Tools:**
+  - `search_archive` over the harvested and candidate articles, using a local full-text index and Atlas Search
+  - `get_article`
+  - `find_death_notices(name, place, window)`
+  - `web_search` through SerpApi, with a budget counter that persists across runs
+  - `wikipedia` for the "now" side when the SerpApi budget runs out (the card says so)
+- **Guardrails in code, not just in the prompt:**
+  - A claim is kept only if it cites at least one clipping and its quote verifies against that clipping. Dropped claims are logged with the reason.
+  - A cause of death is stated only as printed.
+  - The link between a ghost and a death is graded strong, possible or weak, with its reasons listed (name match, place match, date gap).
+- **Output:** a `cases` document, plus one Sentry trace per case with a span per step carrying model, tokens, cost and latency.
+- **Budgets:** a maximum number of steps per case, a maximum number of web searches per case, and a global SerpApi counter (the free plan is 250 searches a month).
+```mermaid
+sequenceDiagram
+  participant W as InvestigateCase workflow
+  participant M as Model activity
+  participant T as Tool activities
+  W->>M: step 1, plan (result recorded)
+  W->>T: step 2, search_archive and find_death_notices (recorded)
+  Note over W: worker killed here
+  W-->>W: replay from history: steps 1 and 2 reuse recorded results
+  W->>M: step 3, write claims
+  W->>T: step 4, verify quotes and save the case file
+### 3.6 Static export and the site
+- `export_static` reads Atlas and writes:
+  - `front.json`: printed-on-this-night candidates, ticker headlines and totals
+  - `towns/index.json`: a compact town index for search on the device
+  - `towns/{place_id}.json` and `cases/{report_id}.json`
+  - `reel.json`: the archive chart
+- The API contract is in `SRS.md` section 6.
+- Both services are defined in `render.yaml`. Nothing deploys until the owner says yes.
+## 4. Data model (MongoDB Atlas, database `paperghosts`)
+Pydantic models in the Python package are the single source of truth. Atlas JSON Schema validators are generated from them.
+**`reports`:** one document per story.
+- `_id`, plus `primary_article_id`
+- `printings[]`: article ID, LCCN, paper title, publication place, state, date, scan location, `bbox_list`, crop URLs
+- `headline`, `text` (the OCR of the primary printing), `date` (earliest printing), `year`, `month_day`
+- `kind` (always `report` in this collection)
+- `fields`: each is `{value, quote, verified, score}`:
+  - `place`
+  - `people[]`
+  - `seen`
+  - `outcome`: unexplained, explained, hoax or unknown
+  - `specific_place`
+  - `place_type`: house, church, cemetery, inn or hotel, road or bridge, public building, ship, or other
+  - `precision`: town, street or building
+- `location`: GeoJSON point, with `location_precision` and `location_source`
+- `place_id`, `town`, `state`
+- `embedding`

+- **Secrets:**

+## 8. Architecture risks and what answers them
+| Risk | Answer |
+| Ingest is limited by CPU, not network | Measure parse speed in Phase 1 and set concurrency from it |
+| Too many candidates for the reader budget | A triage stage measured for recall, plus cost per 10,000 articles and a Tinker credit check before the full pass |
+| Reprints inflate counts and leak gold into training | Reprint clustering, counts labelled as stories or printings, and a leakage check script |
+| Rough OCR | Fuzzy quote verification, and optionally Gemma re-reading the scan image when the OCR is unreadable |
+| LoC image service is slow or down | Lazy loading, cached crops for the top content, and a text fallback |
+| Render free services sleep | The core path is served from static JSON |
+| Atlas free tier is 512 MB | Only stories go to Atlas; the bulk stays local and the article says so |
+| Gemma 4 26B on 24 GB of RAM | Never run it alongside the local student; measure tokens per second in Phase 1 |

+# PRD: Paper Ghosts
+What we are building, for whom, and how we'll know it worked. The full spec is `BRIEF.md`; this file is the product view of it.
+## 1. Summary

+Type a town and read the ghost reports that America's newspapers actually printed there between 1774 and 1963. Each one comes with the original clipping, what happened next, and sometimes the real person behind the ghost.
+Paper Ghosts never writes a ghost story. Everything it shows was printed in a newspaper, and every claim links to the clipping it came from.
+## 2. The problem
+- Real reports are buried in 340 GB of scanned pages that nobody can search by town.
+- People get web legends and ghost-tour retellings instead, and those drift from what was printed.
+- The old Chronicling America JSON API is gone (it returns 404). The archives that remain show pages, not stories.
+## 3. Who it's for
+| Person | What they want |
+| A curious local, on Halloween, on a phone (primary) | "What did the papers say about ghosts in my town?" |
+| A local historian or genealogist | The original source and its follow-ups, with dates and papers, so they can cite it |
+| A ghost-tour guide | What the 1890s paper actually said, next to what the tour says now |
+| A hackathon judge | Proof that it is real, that it works, that the writing is good, and that open models do the real work |
+## 4. Goals and non-goals
+**Goals**
+1. Every US town with a printed report is searchable and returns real clippings.
+2. Every fact on screen carries a quote from its clipping that code has verified.
+3. A small open model trained on Tinker reads the whole archive, with measured accuracy compared against a large teacher and a measured cost per 10,000 articles.
+4. The top cases get case files: follow-ups, debunkings, the person behind the ghost, and then and now.
+5. It feels like a newspaper morgue after hours (`UI-IDEAS.md`), and it is fast on a phone with the lights on or off.
+**Non-goals**
+- Generated stories, AI narration, or invented content anywhere, including screenshots.
+- Accounts, logins, leaderboards or social features.
+- Non-US papers. The lexicon is English, so reports in German, Spanish or other languages are missed; the "What it can't do" section says so.
+- Guesses about causes of death. Private homes as walk stops.
+## 5. Features
+**P0: the vertical slice (must ship)**
+| ID | Feature | Done when |

+| F1 | Town search on a library request slip, leading to the town's drawer: envelopes with typed labels and outcome stamps, a count line, and a small map | A real town returns its real reports, and a town without any says so plainly |

+| F2 | Case page: the clipping under the lamp, the transcription, a raw-OCR toggle, a typed facts card (verified quote or "not stated"), the Library of Congress source link, and **-30-** | Every field on the page traces to a quote in that clipping |
+| F3 | Front page: masthead, search, **Printed on this night** and a ticker of real headlines | Works for any date of the year |
+| F4 | The reel: ghost reports per million articles by year and by state, drawn like an 1870s statistical atlas | Every number comes from the eval A script |
+| F5 | Lights on and off (the pull-chain), phone-first layouts, reduced motion | Passes the checks in `SRS.md` (NFR-A11Y, NFR-PERF) |

+| F6 | The method page: how the archive was read, what it can't do, and the credits the licences require | Credits AmericanStories (CC-BY-4.0), GeoNames (CC-BY), the LoC scans, the map tiles, the fonts and React Bits |
+**P1: depth**
+| ID | Feature |
+| F7 | What happened next: the follow-up clippings on a case page |
+| F8 | The person behind the ghost: the death notice clipped beside the report, with how sure the link is |
+| F9 | Then and now: today's web claims beside the original report, each with its source and retrieval date |
+| F10 | Archive text search with fuzzy matching for OCR errors, where a misread spelling visibly resolves into the word it matched |
+| F11 | Ghosts like this one (vector search) |
+| F12 | Near me: location rounded to about 1 km, used once, never logged |
+**P2:** F13 Walks: self-guided, public stops only, printable. The owner decides at the Phase 4 gate whether it's built.
+**P3:** F14 Road trips, which is the first thing to cut. Optional sound, off by default.
+## 6. Success metrics
+Every result comes from a script in the repo. The targets below are goals; whatever the eval actually says is what gets reported.
+| Area | Metric | Goal |
+| Coverage | Year files read out of 180 | All 180, or each failure listed with its reason |
+| Prefilter | Recall, measured on a random sample and a near-miss pool | Reported with a 95% interval or upper bound |
+| Reader | Report-detection F1 and kind accuracy: tuned 4B against base 4B and the teacher | A clear win over base 4B, with 95% intervals that don't overlap |
+| Reader | Cost per 10,000 articles and latency | Measured for all three models |
+| Grounding | Share of displayed fields with a verified quote | 100%, by construction, plus an audit |
+| Investigations | Case files written, named deaths found, cases explained or exposed, then-and-now differences | 30–60 case files; the other counts are whatever is found |
+| Durability | Kill tests on the ingest and on an investigation | Both resume; no completed paid call is repeated, and any call in flight at the kill is counted |
+| App | Core Web Vitals on a mid-range phone | LCP under 2.5 s, CLS under 0.1, INP under 200 ms |
+| App | Accessibility | No serious axe violations; reading text contrast of at least 4.5:1 in both modes |
+## 7. How it fits the challenge
+**Judging criteria**

+- **Writing quality (weighted most):** the DEV post is a deliverable with its own gate in Phase 5. It is written in the archive librarian's voice and built around the strongest real case the investigator finds. Every number in it comes from the numbers sheet.
+- **Relevance:**
+  - Spooky: real ghost reports.
+  - Honouring the past, in the spirit of Día de los Muertos: the real people behind the ghosts, remembered from their own papers.
+  - Open-weight models do all the reading and investigating.
+- **Creativity:** the newspaper-morgue framing, the person behind the ghost, and then and now (how legends drift from what was printed).
+- **Technical execution:** a full read of 340 GB, durable runs on Temporal, distillation on Tinker with honest evals, and quotes that code verifies.
+- **Partner technology:** each tool has one real job and a piece of proof (`BRIEF.md` "Stack").
+**The four open-angle questions the post answers**
+- **Does it work with the lights and the internet off?** The reader and the investigator run on open weights on the owner's machine, and walks print to paper.
+- **Does it keep things private?** There are no accounts, and near me is rounded and never logged.
+- **Is it free of a service that might disappear?** The data is CC-BY text and public-domain scans, the models are open weights, and crops for the top cases are cached.
+- **Where did open beat closed?** Eval B (cost per 10,000 articles, accuracy gap) and the Gemma against Ultramarine comparison answer it, whichever way the numbers go.

+**Prize categories:** list only those genuinely used at submission time. Tinker is the main one (featured), then Render (featured), Gemma (featured, if the investigator's default stays Gemma 4), MongoDB Atlas, Temporal, Sentry Agent Tracing, SerpApi, Ultramarine and Entire. One win per person, so the depth goes into Tinker.

+- **The voice:** the archive's librarian, plain, dry and exact. No puns, no "spooky", no "unleash", no "dive in".
+- **Respect the dead:** see `BRIEF.md`, non-negotiable 4.
+- **The Halloween look:** it comes from the reading room after dark (the lamp, the lights off, the scans), as `UI-IDEAS.md` describes. No pumpkins, bats, skulls or costume-shop type.

+1. **Walking skeleton (Phase 1):** one real 1850 clipping goes all the way from the archive through Atlas and the API to a web page.
+2. **Each phase deepens its layer** and ends at a gate (`BUILD-PLAN.md`).
+3. **Owner gates, each needing a yes:**

+   - publishing the DEV post

+# SRS: Paper Ghosts
+Software requirements, each with an ID and how it is verified. The gates in `BUILD-PLAN.md` check against these IDs. The product view is in `PRD.md`, and the design is in `ARCHITECTURE.md`.
+## 1. Definitions
+- **Article:** one article region from AmericanStories, with its text, headline, bounding boxes and page.
+- **Printing:** one article as printed in one paper on one date.
+- **Story:** a cluster of printings of the same text. Syndicated stories were reprinted in many papers.
+- **Candidate:** an article that hit the lexicon.
+- **Report:** a candidate the reader classified as `kind = report`.
+- **Case:** a report the investigator worked on.
+- **Clipping:** the crop of the page scan for one article.
+- **Verified quote:** a quote the verifier found in the source text, within the calibrated fuzzy threshold.
+- **Precision:** how exactly a location is known: town, street or building.
+## 2. Functional requirements
+### 2.1 Ingest (ING)
+| ID | Requirement | Verified by |
+| ING-1 | All 180 year files are streamed without ever storing a tarball. Ingest outputs total at most 10 GB on disk. | Per-year manifests, and a disk-use line in eval A |
+| ING-2 | Each year file is one Temporal activity, with heartbeats and a retry policy. Outputs are idempotent. | The Temporal UI history, and kill test 1 |
+| ING-3 | The lexicon is versioned in code, covers common OCR variants, and each candidate records the terms it matched. | Unit tests, including OCR-variant cases |
+| ING-4 | Each year records its pages, articles and candidates, by state and by term. | `eval/results/archive_read.json` |
+| ING-5 | Each year writes a random non-candidate sample and a near-miss pool. | Files exist, and eval A has a recall section |

+| ING-6 | The crop builder handles single-column and multi-column articles (`bbox_list`). It is checked on 50 random candidates spread across as many batches as the sample allows. | `eval/results/crop_check.json`, plus a contact sheet image |
+### 2.2 Reader (RDR)
+| ID | Requirement | Verified by |

+| ID | Requirement | Verified by |
+| DB-1 | Collections and JSON Schema validators are generated from the Pydantic models (`ARCHITECTURE.md` section 4). | `make db-init` is idempotent |

+| INV-1 | The rule that picks the top cases is written down and versioned. | The code, plus `DECISIONS.md` |

+| ID | Requirement | Verified by |
+| WEB-1 | The pages are: front page, town drawer, case, the reel, the method page, a 404 ("This page was never filed."), and walks if they are built. | Playwright e2e |

+| WEB-2 | The design system covers tokens, type, components and brand assets (`BUILD-PLAN.md`, Phase 4A). A style-guide route shows every component, using real archive data only. | Screenshots of the style guide in both modes and at phone width |
+| WEB-3 | The pull-chain switches lights on and off. The default follows the device setting and the time. | e2e |
+| WEB-4 | The seven signature moments from `UI-IDEAS.md` are built, each with its reduced-motion fallback. | e2e with reduced motion emulated |
+| WEB-5 | Layouts are phone-first, and clipping crops are lazy-loaded. The first clipping is the LCP element. | Lighthouse |

+| ID | Requirement | Verified by |

+| ID | Requirement | Verified by |

+- **Machine:** Apple M4 with 10 cores, 24 GB of RAM, and about 35 GB of free disk (measured Oct 29). No Docker.

+- **Installed tools:** `uv`, Node and `pnpm`, the Temporal CLI with its dev server, Ollama (with `gemma4:26b-a4b-it-qat` and smaller Gemma 4 variants already pulled), `gh` and `entire`. Nothing is installed globally; project dependencies go through `uv` and `pnpm`.

+- **Keys:** `.env` holds them; check them by shape only. The names are listed in `BRIEF.md`; the Ultramarine key is `PAPERINSTRUMENTS_API_KEY`. `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` and `TABPFN_TOKEN` are present but unused.
+- **Atlas:** the existing cluster. Its tier and storage limit are recorded in Phase 1.
+## 5. Data requirements
+- **Schemas:** `ARCHITECTURE.md` section 4. Pydantic is the source; Atlas validators are generated from it.
+- **Stable IDs:**
+  - A report is `r_` plus its primary article ID.
+  - A case is `c_` plus its report ID.
+  - A place is its GeoNames ID.
+- **Every derived record** carries the versions that made it (lexicon, prompt, model or adapter, code SHA).
+- **Dates** are ISO 8601. `month_day` is `MM-DD`, used by "Printed on this night".
+- **Text:** the OCR text is stored as printed and is never corrected in place. A cleaned transcription, if one is shown, is stored separately and labelled.
+## 6. API contract (read-only)
+| Method and path | Returns |
+| `GET /api/health` | `{ok, atlas, version}` |
+| `GET /api/places?q=&state=` | Matching towns: `{place_id, name, state, report_count, years}` |
+| `GET /api/towns/{place_id}` | The drawer: the place, its count line, and its reports `{id, date, paper, label, outcome, precision, location}` |
+| `GET /api/reports/{id}` | The full case page payload: the report, plus its case if one exists |
+| `GET /api/search?q=&state=&decade=&page=` | Text-search hits with a snippet, and the misread spellings each hit matched, e.g. `{scanned: "appariiion", term: "apparition"}` |
+| `GET /api/near?lat=&lon=&km=` | Reports near a rounded point. The coordinates are never logged. |
+| `GET /api/reports/{id}/similar?k=` | Vector-search neighbours |
+| `GET /api/tonight?md=MM-DD` | Reports printed on that month and day |
+| `GET /api/stats/reel` | Per-year and per-state series |
+| `GET /api/walks/{place_id}` | A walk (P2 only) |

+### 7.1 Evals A to D
+- **A, the archive read:**
+  - pages and articles read, and candidates per year
+  - reports per million articles, by year and by state
+  - the term mix and an OCR-quality distribution
+  - prefilter recall: a random-sample upper bound (rule of three when no misses are found) and the misses found in the near-miss pool, with the lexicon changes they caused
+- **B, the reader:**
+  - kind accuracy and macro-F1, and report precision, recall and F1
+  - field match rates, and the share of quotes verified
+  - the hallucinated-quote rate
+  - cost per 10,000 articles and latency
+  - bootstrap 95% intervals throughout
+  - the headline is the accuracy gap and the cost per 10,000 articles

+- **C, the investigations:** case files written, named deaths found, cases explained or exposed, then-and-now differences, the claim-verification rate and dropped claims, and Gemma against Ultramarine on the same cases (claims, verification rate, cost, latency).
+- **D, the app:** Lighthouse on mobile, axe, contrast, e2e on phone and desktop in both modes, and the walks counts if walks are built.
+### 7.2 Reader ablations
+| ID | What changes | Why it matters |
+| B1 | Base 4B, tuned 4B, teacher | The headline comparison |
+| B2 | Training set size (a learning curve of at least 3 points) | Whether more teacher labels would help |
+| B3 | LoRA rank and learning rate (a small grid, within credits) | Picks the trained model |
+| B4 | Output format: fields with quotes against kind only | The cost of grounding |
+| B5 | Quote verifier on and off, plus a threshold sweep | Precision of the fields shown |
+| B6 | Triage on and off | Reports lost against cost saved |
+| B7 | Slices by OCR quality | Robustness to rough scans |
+| B8 | Slices by decade | Language drift from 1774 to 1963 |
+| B9 | Base 4B zero-shot against few-shot | Makes the baseline fair |
+| B10 | Reprint leakage removed, or not | Proves the scores aren't inflated |
+Model selection uses a dev split. The gold set is used only for these final runs.
+### 7.3 Edge-case suite
+Each slice uses at least 5 gold items where the archive has them:
+- E1: sermons and hymns about the Holy Ghost
+- E2: idioms ("ghost of a chance", "gave up the ghost", "not the ghost of a")
+- E3: ghost stories as fiction, serials and Christmas stories
+- E4: theatre and illusion adverts (Pepper's ghost), patent medicine and real estate

+- E11: segmentation errors, where several items are merged into one article
+- E12: non-English text
+- E13: "Ghost" as a surname or a place name
+- E14: political figures of speech ("the ghost of the tariff")

# Verification Before Completion

## Overview

**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.

**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
```

If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.

## The Gate Function

```
BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:

1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim

Skip any step = lying, not verifying
```

## Common Failures

| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |

## Red Flags - STOP

- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
- About to commit/push/PR without verification
- Trusting agent success reports
- Relying on partial verification
- Thinking "just this once"
- Tired and wanting work over
- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**

## Rationalization Prevention

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
| "I'm confident" | Confidence ≠ evidence |
| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
| "Linter passed" | Linter ≠ compiler |
| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |
| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |

## Key Patterns

**Tests:**
```
✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
❌ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
```

**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
```
✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)
❌ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
```

**Build:**
```
✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
❌ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
```

**Requirements:**
```
✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion
❌ "Tests pass, phase complete"
```

**Agent delegation:**
```
✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state
❌ Trust agent report
```

## When To Apply

**ALWAYS before:**
- ANY variation of success/completion claims
- ANY expression of satisfaction
- ANY positive statement about work state
- Committing, PR creation, task completion
- Moving to next task
- Delegating to agents

**Rule applies to:**
- Exact phrases
- Paraphrases and synonyms
- Implications of success
- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness
